sections.overview: The Rock Pigeon is a dove that nests on natural cliffs and city ledges. Its close association with people began through domestication thousands of years ago; the familiar urban bird is usually descended from domestic pigeons that escaped or were released. This history has carried feral populations around the world, while genuinely wild populations retain a much narrower native range. The distinction matters because plentiful city flocks do not by themselves show that wild cliff populations are secure.
sections.identification: A typical wild adult is blue-grey, with two black bars across each wing, a white patch on the lower back, and a dark band near the tail tip. Green and purplish iridescence flashes on the neck as the bird turns in the light. Adults usually measure 30–36 cm, weigh 265–380 g and span 50–67 cm; sex and population cause variation. Domestication has produced many colours and patterns, and feral birds may show them too, so a grey, barred individual is not automatically a wild Rock Pigeon.
sections.habitat: The wild native range extends across parts of Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and South Asia, but millennia of domestic movement blur its limits and make some remnant wild populations hard to distinguish from feral birds. Rock Pigeons nest in cliff crevices, usually near open ground where seeds are accessible. Farms provide grain and water, while cliffs offer protected roosts and nest sites. In towns, roofs, bridges and ledges provide similar shelter, explaining urban success without making cities the species’ original home.
sections.diet: The bill picks up seeds and grains from the ground, along with small fruits, green plant material and occasional invertebrates. A pigeon can drink by immersing its bill and drawing water continuously, an unusual ability among birds that avoids repeated head tipping. Swallowed food may pause in the crop, an expandable part of the oesophagus that stores and moistens it. In the glandular stomach (proventriculus), hydrochloric acid activates pepsin for chemical digestion; the muscular gizzard grinds seeds, often aided by swallowed grit, before the small intestine completes digestion and absorbs nutrients. Urban scraps broaden the menu but do not erase the species’ seed-eating biology.
sections.behavior: Outside the breeding season, pigeons often gather to feed and roost. Males bow and coo during courtship, and may regurgitate food to a partner. Experiments on trained homing pigeons show a sun compass corrected by the internal clock and olfactory map cues for locating home after unfamiliar releases; the strength of odor-based navigation varies among regions. GPS-tracked pigeons also follow learned visual routes over familiar terrain. When the sun compass is unavailable, tests support a magnetic compass; these experiments study domestic birds released away from their loft.
sections.reproduction: Pairs may keep the same partner through successive nesting attempts, but long-term bonds can break when breeding conditions change. The male brings twigs while the female arranges them into a loose platform on a ledge or in a cavity. A clutch is usually two white eggs; both adults share incubation for about 18 days, with the male commonly taking the middle of the day. Hatchlings are helpless, sparsely downy nestlings that remain in the nest. Both parents feed crop milk: prolactin stimulates crop-lining cells to multiply and shed, producing a secretion rich in protein and fat but poor in carbohydrates, not milk from mammary glands. Parents gradually add softened or regurgitated seeds as chicks grow. Young usually leave the nest at 25–32 days and continue to be fed as they learn to forage.
sections.ecology: By eating seeds on open ground, Rock Pigeons link wild plants and cultivated grain to the animals that prey on birds. They are themselves taken by predators including Peregrine Falcons; in cities, these raptors sometimes nest on tall buildings and hunt pigeons among the rooftops. Nesting colonies leave conspicuous droppings on building ledges. Their broad diet also lets them exploit food discarded or provided by people, tying local flocks to human activity.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the Rock Pigeon globally as Least Concern. The cited assessment is the 2016 version amended in 2019. That broad category can obscure a problem for wild birds: domestic and feral pigeons interbreed with cliff-dwelling Rock Pigeons, introducing genes and sometimes replacing local ancestry. Research in Britain and Ireland found the least introgression in the Outer Hebrides and varying admixture elsewhere; plumage alone cannot reliably identify an individual’s ancestry. The 2021 European Red List assessment classed the species as Least Concern but its regional population trend was unknown. Cornell’s North American summary reported a 46% decline from 1966 to 2015, a regional signal rather than a global estimate.
